newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Feb 25.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Feb 25.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- SIB TOP JOB SELECTION DELAYED BY LABOUR

Shadow Chancellor Gordon Brown has delayed the appointment of a new chairman of the Securities and Investments Board, the City regulator, because he was unhappy about the selection process. Brown was consulted by Chancellor Kenneth Clarke because of the possibility of Labour winning the general election. The final selection of who heads SIB will be made jointly by the governor of the Bank of England and whoever is chancellor.
-- AVIS AND UBS IN PROFITS ROW

Avis Europe and UBS, the stockbrokers, are involved in a row over the car rental company's future. UBS Securities is co-leader of the syndicate of City firms floating Avis Europe but has suggested the company's profits will be much lower than other brokers' estimates. Avis Europe claims that UBS has made a mistake by failing to indicate the effect of the 250 million stg the company hopes to raise in the 700 million stg floatation.
THE TIMES
-- YORKSHIRE ELECTRICITY ACCEPTS 1.5 BILLION STG US OFFER

Yorkshire Electricity has accepted a 1.5 billion stg takeover offer from Yorkshire Holdings, a company equally owned by American Electric Power of Ohio and Public Services of Colorado. Seven of the regional electricity companies are now under American control with only Southern Electric remaining independent. Analysts believe the bid is fairly valued and do not expect a rival takeover offer.
-- SB AGREES 325 MILLION DOLLAR AMERICAN SETTLEMENT

Britain's second largest pharmaceutical group, SmithKline Beecham, has agreed settle a dispute with American regulators, the Department of Justice and the Office of the Inspector General of the Department of Health, by paying 325 million dollars. The regulators had accused the company's Clinical Laboratories division of charging for blood and urine tests that were either unautorised or medically unnecessary between 1989 and 1996.
-- FULL STEAM AHEAD FOR HALIFAX

A 97 percent majority of Halifax members have voted in favour of the proposed conversion into a bank, set for June. The society's stock market debut will be the widest-ever extension of share ownership, benefiting one in five households in the UK. The Halifax is giving out shares in two tranches, the basic and variable division. The distribution of 200 shares will be given to members who had at least 100 stg in their account at November 25, 1994, and February 24, 1997, and to qualifying borrowers.
THE GUARDIAN
-- GLOBAL WARMING FEARS ADD IMPETUS TO SOLAR POWER

The world's biggest insurance companies are backing efforts to turn solar power into a viable competitor to coal, oil and gas, due to fears of multi-billion stg damages claims caused by global warming. Fifty companies, including some of Britain's biggest banks, attended the Solar Oxford Investment Summit, and agreed to help accelerate the commercial market for producing electricity from sunlight.
-- SHELL FACES CHALLENGE FROM SHAREHOLDERS

Shell's annual meeting in May will see a group of shareholders pressing Shell to publish regular audits of the group's social and environmental performance. Pirc, the pensions industry research organisation, has secured the backing of 100 shareholders for a resolution aimed at the oil group's difficulties over the Brent Spar oil platform and its involvement in Nigeria. Pirc and Shell have been in discussion since 1994, when its environmental concerns were first expressed.
-- HANSON ERA ENDS ON ENERGETIC HIGH NOTE

The Energy Group, which comprises Eastern Electricity and Peabody, the US coal company, has joined the stock market, announcing a 38 percent rise in operating profits and seeing its shares rise sharply. This signifies the completion of the break-up of Hanson. Derek Bonham, chairman, resigned as director of Hanson, and said the profits at the Energy Group had soared because of the acquisition of power stations from National Power and PowerGen.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- NEW-LOOK GUS GETS FINANCE DIRECTOR

David Tyler is to become the first finance director for a decade at Great Universal Stores, the mail order group presently being shaken-up by new chairman Lord Wolfson. Following a one billion stg acquisition of US data company Experian, GUS has become more active in the corporate arena, therefore a more traditional board structure has become more appropriate. Other boardroom appointments at GUS are David Bury, who becomes commercial director and treasurer, and Louise Patten, who joins as non-executive director.
-- THORN TO AXE 360 AT RENTALS DIVISION

Thorn, in an effort to improve efficiency, is set to close 90 branches of its Radio Rentals chain and cut 360 jobs. Following its demerger from Thorn EMI last August the company has seen poor trading and a sliding share price, and will now re-structure its central support functions in the UK to cut costs. It is introducing several promotional schemes in America designed to improve sales and encourage customer loyalty. This comes as City speculation mounts regarding possible management changes.
